provenance.setting: An English yeoman farmstead family (Tudor/farmstead vernacular) on pastured lowland with a small stone quarry, managed oak coppice, and a sawpit — the cottage and the tithe barn are both buildings of this one place, so they draw on the same materials.

sources.local-fieldstone: Rubble fieldstone cleared from the surrounding pasture — abundant and cheap; irregular, mottled grey; laid uncoursed for wall fields and chimney shafts.
sources.quarried-ashlar: Dressed stone from the small local quarry — costly to cut, so it is spent only where it earns its keep: quoins, buttress piers, plinth courses, door and window dressings.
sources.oak-coppice: Dark structural oak from the managed coppice — heavy hewn frame timbers (posts, studs, bressummers, joists) and the dark weathered edge boards.
sources.sawn-softwood: Lighter sawn boards from the sawpit — roof plank courses, door leaves, shutters, and lattice fills; warm medium browns, flatter grain than the frame oak.
sources.lime-render: Lime plaster over wattle — the cream infill panels between upper-storey frame timbers; never used at ground level where rain-splash erodes it.
sources.clay-bricks: A small batch of kiln-fired brick — expensive and fire-safe, reserved for chimney caps above the roof line.

provenance.wealthClass: Yeoman — dressed stone at corners and openings, cheap fieldstone elsewhere; no slate, no glass larger than a lattice pane.
provenance.roofingEconomy: Sawn timber plank/shingle roofs at the steep 45° pitch class; ridge and eave edges boarded in the darker oak.

palette.rationale: Ground-storey wall fields are the cheap material: uncoursed rubble fieldstone (the barn's recessed panels; the vernacular default a concept may override with dressed stone, as the cottage's ashlar ground storey does).

Quoins, buttress piers, plinth courses, jambs and heads are dressed quarry stone — crisp coursed blocks spent only where structure or weather demands them (the cottage/barn near-tone grey pair, kept distinct from the rubble field).
The half-timber frame — corner posts, studs, eaves beams — is heavy coppice oak with visible round grain; near-black against the cream panels it carries.
Upper-storey panels between the frame timbers are lime plaster over wattle — warm matte cream, never pure white, never used at ground level (rain-splash).

Roof slopes are sawpit plank courses — warm medium brown, flatter grain and clearly lighter than the frame oak (the cottage roof field; a concept may darken the whole roof toward the oak, as the barn does).
Eaves, verge and rake fascia are boarded in the darker oak — the deep edge banding both concepts show over the lighter roof field (and the barn's whole-roof dominant).
The stepped roof course realization of the sawn-plank field — the stair member of the roof family the generators emit.
The half-step member of the roof family — shallow-pitch landings and ridge half-caps.
Chimney caps are the one brick element — fire-safe kiln brick crowning the cool fieldstone shaft, warm-on-cool (the cottage's red cap).
Door leaves are sawn boards — warm panelled timber set in stone reveals.
Barn wagon-door leaves are bright golden sawn boarding — the lighter, warmer timber kept distinct from the dark roof above (the barn's opening fill).
Shutters and slatted window fills are coppice-oak lattice — the gridded reveal both storeys of the cottage show.
Open lattice fills for unglazed lights — thin sawn members reading as leaded/lattice grid.
